analysis.one_liner: Ends the insurance industry's exemption from federal price-fixing and monopoly laws.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill in October 1990, but the House never voted on it before the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, federal antitrust laws—the rules against price fixing and monopolies—have not applied to insurance companies under a law called the McCarran-Ferguson Act. This bill would strip that protection for four specific practices: fixing prices, agreeing with competitors on who sells insurance where, forcing customers to buy one type of insurance to get another, and monopolizing markets. It would keep allowing insurers to share historical claims data and use actuaries, since that joint statistical work does not itself raise prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy auto, home, health, and business insurance. When insurers are immune from antitrust law, they can legally agree on prices through industry rate-setting groups and divide up markets without facing antitrust suits. Making price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization illegal under federal law would let regulators, state enforcers, and private plaintiffs challenge those practices, aiming to bring premiums down and keep companies from carving up markets.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption for four specific insurance practices: price fixing, allocating markets with competitors, tying one insurance product to another, and monopolizing or attempting to monopolize any part of the business.
Federal antitrust law would now reach these practices even in states that regulate insurance, because the exemption ends for this conduct whether or not state law regulates it.

Includes a transition period—one to two years depending on insurer size—before the rules fully apply, and preserves joint collection of historical loss data, loss development factors, trend factors, and actuarial services, so routine statistical cooperation among insurers stays legal.
The bill took effect one year after enactment, giving insurers time to adjust their pricing practices.

analysis.who_pays: Insurance companies, which would lose legal immunity for price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization and could face federal antitrust lawsuits, penalties, and private damages claims for conduct that has been lawful under the exemption since 1945.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurance companies and industry rate bureaus

drawbacks.text: State insurance regulators and insurers have long argued that federal antitrust enforcement would duplicate or clash with state rate regulation, creating years of litigation over pricing practices that state regulators have approved.

Even with the carve-outs, insurers would bear new legal risk and litigation costs, which some argue could be passed on to policyholders and could discourage the joint statistical work that lets smaller insurers price coverage accurately.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was drawn narrowly: it targeted only hard-core antitrust violations—price fixing, market division, tying, and monopolization—while explicitly protecting the shared data collection and actuarial work insurers say they need, and it gave the industry a phase-in period. The main cost is litigation and adjustment expense for insurers; the main benefit is that premiums would no longer be set through conduct the rest of the economy treats as illegal. The strongest objection—that federal antitrust would collide with state regulation—is a design question, but the bill addressed the main one by keeping routine data sharing exempt.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee for over a year and a half, was approved by the House Judiciary Committee in late October 1990, and was placed on the House calendar, but the House leadership never scheduled a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Jack Brooks and Don Edwards introduced the bill on April 4, 1989, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
The Judiciary Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law held hearings in July 1989 and April 1990.
On June 13, 1990, the subcommittee amended the bill and forwarded it to the full committee, which ordered it reported on June 20, 1990.
The full Judiciary Committee reported the bill with amendments on October 27, 1990, as House Report 101-976.
The bill was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills eligible for floor action, but no floor vote ever occurred before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurance companies came out ahead: they kept the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption for price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization because the House never voted on the bill. Consumers gained nothing, since the repeal died without ever reaching a vote.

against.name: Insurance industry
against.role: Insurers and industry trade groups benefiting from the McCarran-Ferguson exemption
against.what_they_did: Opposed narrowing the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption, which since 1945 has shielded insurance rate-setting and market practices from federal antitrust suits.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced and advanced entirely by House Democrats—Brooks, Edwards, and all seven cosponsors—with no Republican cosponsor listed, and it never reached a floor vote where the parties' positions would have been recorded.

industries.note: The bill would end their exemption from federal antitrust law for price fixing, dividing up markets, tying products, and monopolizing, exposing conduct that has been lawful under McCarran-Ferguson since 1945 to antitrust suits. The industry's interest in keeping the exemption runs directly against insurance buyers, who pay premiums set under that shield.

The bill keeps the antitrust exemption for collecting and sharing historical loss data, computing loss development and trend factors, and actuarial services, so the industry's joint statistical machinery stays legal. But the pricing and market agreements that bureaus historically facilitated would no longer be exempt.

State regulation of insurance continues, and the bill applies federal antitrust to hard-core conduct even in regulated states. Regulators who relied on the McCarran-Ferguson framework to keep rate regulation exclusively at the state level would see federal enforcers and private plaintiffs active in their territory.
